summary:
PARALLAX treats SPHEREx’s time dimension as a new way to find faint moving objects and test microlensing. SPHEREx records a different wavelength in each exposure and revisits the sky every six months. Most tools treat that wavelength change as a nuisance; PARALLAX models time and wavelength together.

Type any sky position and the Observatory finds every SPHEREx exposure covering it, straight from NASA’s public archive. It plays them in time order, labelled with wavelength, detector and time, and lets you compare epochs. On real data it measures the proper motion of Barnard’s Star from SPHEREx alone.

Its search stacks frames along trial orbits while matching spectral templates. In simulations it finds cold, brown-dwarf-like objects (the kind a Planet X search targets) 0.65 magnitudes fainter than standard stacking, at the same false-alarm rate. A Gravity mode tests microlensing against stellar variability using the colour of the brightening, and gives an honest estimate of how many events SPHEREx can expect.
details:
What it does?

Observatory: turns any RA/Dec into a time-ordered animation of every SPHEREx Level-2 exposure covering it. Each frame is labelled with wavelength, detector, UTC and observation ID. It offers epoch comparison, flux-matched difference images, co-adds, per-pixel spectra and light curves, and proper-motion fitting.

Motion: a matched filter over trial trajectories × a bank of spectral templates, using the archive’s own PSF, variance and wavelength maps. Thresholds are set on null fields, and it is compared fairly against shift-and-stack, per-detector stacking and detect-then-link.

Gravity: fits a point-lens light curve with separate spectra for the lensed star and for blended neighbours. It compares that against constant-source and symmetric-variable models. It gives no verdict when no model fits adequately, and a lens verdict also needs physically valid parameters.

Results:

Barnard’s Star (real data): 238 exposures found from one position, with motion detected at 7σ. Each visit agrees with the Gaia DR3 prediction to within 1.2″, about 0.2 pixel.

Search depth (simulated): +0.65 magnitudes for cold spectra and about 0 for reflected sunlight, which is what theory predicts.

Lens vs variable star (simulated):

The guarded rule calls 0 of 100 variable stars a lens; the score alone called 30.

The event timescale is 2.8× more accurate than a single-colour fit.

It does not detect more events.

Feasibility: SPHEREx deep fields should see about 0.02 lensing events per year or fewer, so SPHEREx is a follow-up tool for known events.

Impact:

Anyone, including students, the public and researchers, can explore SPHEREx’s time dimension at any position without downloading whole images. It also gives a tested, honest method for spectrum-aware searches for faint movers.

Tools:

Python (NumPy, SciPy, Astropy, httpx, FastAPI, Uvicorn, pytest) and a vanilla JavaScript front end with no build step. It reads only the needed parts of each FITS file over HTTP, so it works even while the IRSA search service is down. Fetched data is cached, so the demo fields work offline.

What makes it creative?

It treats the wavelength changing between frames as a signal for both motion and lensing.

Factors we considered:

Fair baselines.

Null-calibrated false-alarm rates.

Clear labelling of real vs simulated results.

Negative results reported (the branch-and-bound speed-up pruned nothing).
